function.name: generate_image_tool
function.description: Generates an image based on the provided description and saves it with the specified file name. The image description should be detailed to ensure the resulting image matches the desired subject and surroundings; otherwise, these aspects will be chosen randomly. This function is not intended for generating images from textual data. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

desc.description: A single string that provides a detailed description of the desired image. For example, 'a sunset over the mountains with a lake in the foreground'.

file_name.description: The name of the file to which the generated image will be saved. It should include the file extension, such as 'image.png'.

function.name: tts_tool
function.description: Converts the provided text content to speech and saves the resulting audio to a file. This function is intended for voice narration and should be used accordingly. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

content.description: The text content that needs to be converted to speech.

speaker.description: The voice to be used for the text-to-speech conversion.

file_name.description: The name of the file to save the audio output without the extension. If left empty, a default name will be generated based on the content.

This function should be used when there is a need to persist text data in Markdown format as a result of a user action or a process that requires saving information in a structured text file. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

content.description: The Markdown formatted text content to be written to the file.

filename.description: The name of the file to which the Markdown content will be written. If not provided, a default filename will be used.

function.description: Writes an HTML file to disk with the given content. Ensures HTML tags within the content are properly closed. This function should be used when there is a need to save HTML content to a file as part of a 'save' operation. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

content.description: The HTML content to be written to the file. Must contain valid HTML structure.

filename.description: The name of the file to which the HTML content will be written. If not provided, a default filename will be used.

function.name: search_web_tool
function.description: Executes a search query using the DuckDuckGo search engine and returns a specified number of search results from a given source. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

query.description: The search term or phrase to be queried.

num_results.description: The maximum number of search results to return. A positive integer.

source.description: The source from which the search results should be fetched.

function.name: get_url_content
function.description: Scrapes the specified URL for textual data and returns the content as a string. This function is useful for extracting information from web pages when a URL is provided. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

url.description: The web address of the page to scrape. It should be a valid URL format, such as 'http://www.example.com'.

timeout.description: The maximum time in seconds to wait for the server to send data before giving up, with a default value that allows for a reasonable amount of time for most web pages to load.

user_agent.description: The User-Agent string to be used for the HTTP request to simulate a particular browser, which is optional. Some websites may require this for access.

message.content:
Below is a **complete, ready‑to‑run** example that shows how to create a Google Cloud Compute Engine instance that has an NVIDIA RTX A6000 GPU and runs Ubuntu 20.04 LTS.  
The example uses the `gcloud` command‑line tool (the easiest way to interact with the Compute Engine REST API).  
If you prefer to use the raw REST API, the same parameters are shown in the JSON payload at the end.

> **Prerequisites**  
> * You have a Google Cloud project with billing enabled.  
> * The Compute Engine API is enabled (`gcloud services enable compute.googleapis.com`).  
> * You have the `gcloud` SDK installed and authenticated (`gcloud auth login`).  
> * You have the **NVIDIA GPU Driver** installed on the instance after it boots (see the “Post‑creation steps” section).

---

## 1. Pick a zone that supports RTX A6000 GPUs

Not all zones support all GPU types.  
Use the following command to list zones that support the `nvidia-tesla-a6000` accelerator:

```bash
gcloud compute accelerator-types list --filter="name:nvidia-tesla-a6000" --format="table(name,zone)"
```

Choose one of the zones that appears in the output (e.g., `us-central1-a`, `europe-west4-a`, etc.).

---

## 2. Create the instance

```bash
# Variables – replace these with your own values
PROJECT_ID="my-gcp-project"
ZONE="us-central1-a"          # <-- pick a zone that supports RTX A6000
INSTANCE_NAME="rtx-a6000-ubuntu"
MACHINE_TYPE="n1-standard-8" # 8 vCPUs, 30 GB RAM – adjust as needed
GPU_COUNT=1                   # Number of RTX A6000 GPUs

# Create the instance
gcloud compute instances create "$INSTANCE_NAME" \
    --project="$PROJECT_ID" \
    --zone="$ZONE" \
    --machine-type="$MACHINE_TYPE" \
    --accelerator="type=nvidia-tesla-a6000,count=$GPU_COUNT" \
    --image-family="ubuntu-2004-lts" \
    --image-project="ubuntu-os-cloud" \
    --boot-disk-size="100GB" \
    --boot-disk-type="pd-ssd" \
    --metadata-from-file startup-script=startup.sh \
    --tags=http-server,https-server \
    --scopes=https://www.googleapis.com/auth/cloud-platform
```

### Explanation of the flags

| Flag | Purpose |
|------|---------|
| `--machine-type` | CPU/RAM configuration. `n1-standard-8` gives 8 vCPUs & 30 GB RAM. |
| `--accelerator` | Adds the GPU. Format: `type=<GPU_TYPE>,count=<NUM>` |
| `--image-family` & `--image-project` | Uses the latest Ubuntu 20.04 LTS image from the official Ubuntu Cloud image project. |
| `--boot-disk-size` & `--boot-disk-type` | SSD boot disk of 100 GB. |
| `--metadata-from-file startup-script=startup.sh` | Optional: runs a shell script on first boot (see below). |
| `--tags` | Opens ports 80/443 if you plan to run a web server. |
| `--scopes` | Grants the instance full Cloud Platform access (needed for installing drivers). |

---

## 3. Install NVIDIA GPU drivers automatically

Google Cloud offers a **startup script** that installs the NVIDIA driver automatically.  
Create a file named `startup.sh` in the same directory as your command:

```bash
#!/bin/bash
# Install NVIDIA driver
sudo apt-get update
sudo apt-get install -y nvidia-driver-535
# Reboot so the driver loads
sudo reboot
```

Make sure the script is executable:

```bash
chmod +x startup.sh
```

When the instance boots for the first time, the script will run, install the driver, and reboot.  
After the reboot, the GPU will be available for CUDA workloads.

> **Tip:** If you need a specific driver version, replace `nvidia-driver-535` with the desired package name (e.g., `nvidia-driver-525`).

---

## 4. Verify the GPU is visible

SSH into the instance:

```bash
gcloud compute ssh "$INSTANCE_NAME" --zone="$ZONE"
```

Once logged in, run:

```bash
nvidia-smi
```

You should see a table listing the RTX A6000 GPU, its driver version, and usage statistics.

---

## 5. (Optional) Using the REST API directly

If you prefer to call the Compute Engine REST API directly (e.g., from a script or program), the equivalent JSON payload looks like this:

```json
{
  "name": "rtx-a6000-ubuntu",
  "machineType": "zones/us-central1-a/machineTypes/n1-standard-8",
  "disks": [
    {
      "boot": true,
      "autoDelete": true,
      "initializeParams": {
        "sourceImage": "projects/ubuntu-os-cloud/global/images/family/ubuntu-2004-lts",
        "diskSizeGb": 100,
        "diskType": "projects/my-gcp-project/zones/us-central1-a/diskTypes/pd-ssd"
      }
    }
  ],
  "accelerators": [
    {
      "acceleratorCount": 1,
      "acceleratorType": "projects/my-gcp-project/zones/us-central1-a/acceleratorTypes/nvidia-tesla-a6000"
    }
  ],
  "metadata": {
    "items": [
      {
        "key": "startup-script",
        "value": "#!/bin/bash\nsudo apt-get update\nsudo apt-get install -y nvidia-driver-535\nsudo reboot"
      }
    ]
  },
  "networkInterfaces": [
    {
      "network": "global/networks/default",
      "accessConfigs": [
        {
          "type": "ONE_TO_ONE_NAT",
          "name": "External NAT"
        }
      ]
    }
  ],
  "serviceAccounts": [
    {
      "email": "default",
      "scopes": ["https://www.googleapis.com/auth/cloud-platform"]
    }
  ],
  "tags": {
    "items": ["http-server", "https-server"]
  }
}
```

Send this payload to the Compute Engine Instances insert endpoint:

```
POST https://compute.googleapis.com/compute/v1/projects/{project}/zones/{zone}/instances
```

Replace `{project}` and `{zone}` with your project ID and chosen zone.

---

## 6. Clean up

When you’re done, delete the instance to avoid incurring charges:

```bash
gcloud compute instances delete "$INSTANCE_NAME" --zone="$ZONE" --quiet
```

---

### Summary

1. **Pick a zone** that supports RTX A6000.  
2. Run the `gcloud compute instances create` command with the appropriate flags.  
3. Optionally supply a startup script to install NVIDIA drivers automatically.  
4. Verify with `nvidia-smi`.  

That’s all you need to spin up a GPU‑enabled Compute Engine instance with an RTX A6000 and Ubuntu 20.04 LTS!
